Sever
sev'-ēr
v. (to separate, to divide, to set apart from)
Latin separare, to separate, through Old French sevrer. In Scripture God is nearly always the one who severs, and He does it twice in Exodus to distinguish His people in the middle of a judgment.

Biblical Definition

In the plagues God twice announces a severing. “I will sever in that day the land of Goshen, in which my people dwell, that no swarms of flies shall be there; to the end thou mayest know that I am the LORD in the midst of the earth” (Exo 8:22). And of the murrain: “the LORD shall sever between the cattle of Israel and the cattle of Egypt: and there shall nothing die of all that is the children's of Israel” (Exo 9:4). The stated purpose is revelation — to the end thou mayest know. The severing is not merely protective; it is evidential, a line drawn through a country so that everyone can see there is a God who distinguishes. The final severing is our Lord's, at the end of the parable of the net: “So shall it be at the end of the world: the angels shall come forth, and sever the wicked from among the just” (Mat 13:49). Note the direction — the wicked are severed from among the just, which assumes they were mixed together until then, exactly as the tares grew with the wheat and the bad fish came up in the same net. The separation is at the end, it is performed by angels and not by men, and it is final. Ezekiel adds a grim administrative use: men “of continual employment” severed out to bury the dead of Gog's army and cleanse the land (Eze 39:14).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines sever as to part or divide by violence, to separate by parting or rending; and to separate one thing from another, to disjoin.

expand to see more

SEVER, v.t. To part or divide by violence; to separate by parting or rending; as, to sever the body or the arm at a single stroke.

1. To part from the rest by violence; as, to sever the head from the body.

2. To separate and put in a different order or place; as, the angels shall sever the wicked from among the just.

3. To disjoin; to disunite; in a general sense, but usually implying violence.

Key Scripture

Mat 13:49 — "So shall it be at the end of the world: the angels shall come forth, and sever the wicked from among the just,"

Exo 8:22 — "And I will sever in that day the land of Goshen, in which my people dwell, that no swarms of flies shall be there; to the end thou mayest know that I am the LORD in the midst of the earth."

Exo 9:4 — "And the LORD shall sever between the cattle of Israel and the cattle of Egypt: and there shall nothing die of all that is the children's of Israel."

Eze 39:14 — "And they shall sever out men of continual employment, passing through the land to bury with the passengers those that remain upon the face of the earth, to cleanse it:"

Modern Corruption

The final separation is denied or brought forward; Scripture says the angels do it, at the end, out of a mixed field.

expand to see more

Two errors run opposite ways from Matthew 13:49. The first denies the severing altogether, insisting that a God of love makes no final division — against which our Lord's own parables of the tares, the net and the sheep and the goats stand immovable, all of them ending in a separation He performs. The second brings the severing forward and gives it to men: the sect that believes it can produce a pure church now by sufficiently rigorous exclusion. The parable of the tares forbids it explicitly — let both grow together until the harvest — not because purity does not matter but because we cannot tell the plants apart without uprooting wheat.

This is not an argument against church discipline, which the same Lord commands in Matthew 18 and Paul enforces in 1 Corinthians 5. Discipline deals with open, unrepented sin in a professing member and aims at his restoration; it never claims to be the final judgment. The distinction is the whole of a healthy ecclesiology: the church judges what is visible and leaves the heart to the One who reads it, knowing that the angels will do at the end of the world what no eldership can do now.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew palah (H6395), to distinguish, to set apart; badal (H914), to divide, to separate; Greek aphorizo (G873), to mark off by a boundary.

expand to see more

Hebrew palah (H6395) — to distinguish, to make a distinction, to set apart; Exodus 8:22, 9:4, 11:7, 33:16.

Hebrew badal (H914) — to divide, to separate; Genesis 1:4 (light from darkness), Leviticus 20:24-26 (Israel from the nations).

Greek aphorizo (G873) — to separate, to mark off by boundaries; Matthew 13:49, 25:32, of the sheep from the goats.

Greek sunteleia tou aionos (G4930, G165) — the end of the age or world; the appointed time of the severing.

Greek zizanion (G2215) — tares; the parable that forbids an early separation by human hands.

Usage

"“The angels shall come forth, and sever the wicked from among the just”."

"“I will sever in that day the land of Goshen” — that thou mayest know."

"“The LORD shall sever between the cattle of Israel and the cattle of Egypt”."
